item.title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
item.dc:creator: Kevin Shabahang
item.description: Learn how i14 trained and served Laplace 3B, a linear attention model, on AWS Trainium2 using native PyTorch. Its recurrent state stays fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence regardless of context length, avoiding the growing key-value cache of transformer models and keeping serving memory predictable.
item.content:encoded:
Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history.

i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2. This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer.

On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results.

About i14

i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token.

Why linear attention models?

Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens.

Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O(T2) to O(T) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence.

Consideration Transformer softmax attention Laplace 3B with GLA
Training attention Builds pairwise token scores with O(T2) scaling Updates chunked recurrent state with O(T) scaling
Inference memory KV cache grows with context Recurrent state remains fixed in size
Longer contexts Each sequence consumes more accelerator memory Context length does not increase recurrent-state allocation
Implementation Uses widely optimized attention kernels Requires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning

Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements.

How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2

The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, because it performed better.

The implementation required three changes:

  1. Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer.
  2. Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times.
  3. Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler.

The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail.

Why AWS Trainium accelerators?

AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. A trn2.48xlarge instance combines 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 logical NeuronCores, high-bandwidth memory, and NeuronLink-v3 connectivity. These resources support the distributed training and inference configurations described in this post.

Three properties of Trainium2 shaped the implementation: software-managed on-chip memory (Challenge 1), a fast chip-to-chip interconnect (Challenge 2), and a static compiler (Challenge 3). The compiler traces the GLA recurrence as a fixed graph.

Software-managed on-chip memory. Each NeuronCore has a 28 MiB State Buffer (SBUF) with 128 partitions and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM). The PSUM is wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine, alongside separate vector and scalar units. The SBUF is not a cache: the compiler schedules every HBM-to-SBUF transfer ahead of time, so the data is in place with no evictions or misses (Figure 1).

Figure 1: NeuronCore-v3 internal architecture. Software-managed SBUF (28 MiB, 128 partitions), Tensor Engine (128×128 systolic array), Vector Engine, Scalar Engine, and GPSIMD cores.

i14 and the Laplace 3B architecture

Laplace 3B is the 24-layer i14 decoder, where every layer replaces softmax attention with Simple GLA. Figure 2 follows one layer from the input xt at the top to the output xt + 1 at the bottom. This section explains each module: normalization and convolution, the QKVG projection, the GLA mixer, and the feed-forward channel mixer.

Normalization and convolution. Each token’s residual-stream vector xt ∈ ℝD (D = 3, 072) passes through a LayerNorm and a depth-wise causal Conv1d of width k = 4 with SiLU. This gives every position a 4-gram summary before the mixer. The GLA mixer then does content-based retrieval over the whole history through its decaying state.

QKVG projection. The post-conv output goes through one fused matrix Wqkvg ∈ ℝ9, 216 × 3, 072, where 9, 216 = H × (2dk + 2dv). It splits into four per-token streams: queries qt, keys kt, values vt, and a gate gt (H = 16, dk = 96, dv = 192). The gate is used after the mixer.

Figure 2: Laplace decoder layer architecture. Green = fixed (no params), gray = learned, yellow = recurrent state, blue = projection.

GLA mixer. Each head h keeps a matrix state St(h) of size dk × dv (96 × 192), a compressed, decaying record of past key-value pairs. At each token, it updates as:

GLA recurrent-state update equation


Here λh is the fixed per-head decay, and ktvt⊤ is the rank-1 outer product that writes the current key-value pair into the state. The readout queries the state:

GLA state-readout equation


Next, a self-augmentation step adds a gated copy of the value to each head’s output:

GLA self-augmentation equation


Here σ is the sigmoid and ⊙ is the element-wise product. The gate is the query dotted with a learned per-channel rescaling of the key, where a is the learned scale (aug_balance). At initialization, a = 0, which gives a half-strength skip of the value. The per-head outputs pass through a Head RMSNorm within each decay tier, are concatenated, gated by SiLU(gt), and projected by Wout ∈ ℝD × D back to the residual stream.

Decay schedule. The per-head decay rate λh controls how fast a head forgets past tokens. It is fixed at initialization (not learned) and set by a geometric schedule. The schedule gives the 16 heads a spread of memory lengths and defines each head’s log-decay rate γh:

GLA decay schedule equations


Decay schedule’s reach. For this model, Tmin = 1 and Tmax = 2, 048. Head 0 therefore has λ0 = 0.5 (half-life of one token), and head 15 has λ15 ≈ 0.9997 (half-life of 2,048 tokens). Heads are grouped into tiers, each sharing a Head RMSNorm.

Channel mixer (FFN). After the attention block and its residual, a second LayerNorm feeds a GLU (SiLU) FFN with inner dimension 8,192. Its three matrices are two up-projections W1, W2 ∈ ℝ8, 192 × D and one down-projection W3 ∈ ℝD × 8, 192. A second residual follows.

The state S(h) is fixed at dk × dv = 96 × 192 per head regardless of sequence length. As a result, inference is O(1) per token, and training is O(T) rather than O(T2).

Parameter Value
Parameters 3.028B total (2.718B Muon + 309.6M AdamW)
Layers 24 decoder layers, D = 3, 072 hidden dim
Heads 16 heads, dk = 96 (half-width Q/K), dv = 192 (full-width V)
Mixer Simple GLA with fixed geometric decay (Tmin = 1, Tmax = 2, 048)
Conv Depth-wise causal Conv1d, kernel width 4, SiLU
FFN GLU (SiLU), inner dim 8,192
Norm LayerNorm pre-attn + Head RMSNorm (per tier) + LayerNorm pre-FFN
Vocab 50,304 (padded to multiple of 64)
Sequence 2,048
Training data 100B tokens, FineWeb-Edu
Optimizer Muon for 2D weight matrices; AdamW for embeddings, norms
Batch size 524,288 tokens/step, cosine LR, 3,815-step warmup

Engineering challenges

Each of the three changes raised its own engineering challenge.

Challenge 1: Using native PyTorch on Trainium for GLA

On GPU, GLA runs as the fused Triton kernel fused_chunk_simple_gla from the flash-linear-attention library. The GenAIIC team re-expressed it with standard PyTorch operators running through TorchNeuron Native, as explicit loops over fixed-size chunks. The chunk count is fixed at compile time and sets the backward-unroll depth. The team uses fla_num_chunks = 16, so each chunk holds C = 128 tokens.

Within each chunk c, the intra-chunk output is masked linear attention, and the running state S adds earlier context:

Chunked GLA intra-chunk output

The state then advances to the next chunk:

Chunked GLA state update

Here λC is the per-head decay compounded over the chunk. The 16 intra-chunk computations run in parallel, and only the state update is sequential (Figure 3).

Figure 3: GLA chunked recurrence with parallel intra-chunk attention and a sequential state chain.

Because the SBUF has 128 partitions, each 128-token chunk maps one token per partition, with no padding or cross-partition movement. This alignment increased measured throughput by 14 percent (Figure 4).

Figure 4: Chunk size C = 128 maps one-to-one onto the 128 SBUF partitions.

Challenge 2: Distributed Muon orthogonalization under FSDP2

Muon orthogonalizes each gradient before the update. For each of the 96 two-dimensional weight matrices (2.718 billion parameters), it runs five Newton–Schulz iterations (Algorithm 1).

The Newton-Schulz algorithm

The distributed problem. The Gram matrix A = XX⊤ correlates every row of the weight with every other row. Under Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2), each of the 64 ranks holds only 1/64 of the rows. A shard-local XX⊤ therefore yields only a diagonal block and drops every cross-shard term (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Newton–Schulz under FSDP2: the shard-local Gram block, and gather/broadcast compared with all_to_all.

Naive approach: Gather and broadcast. Every rank gathers the full gradient (5.44 GB), one rank runs Newton–Schulz, and it broadcasts the result. This moves 10.87 GB per step while the other 63 ranks wait.

Production approach: all_to_all transposition. In MuonFSDP2, one all_to_all gives each rank a few complete matrices, all 64 ranks run Newton–Schulz in parallel, and a second all_to_all returns the results. Per-rank traffic drops to 0.45 GB, 24 times less. Throughput rises from 73,378 to 119,934 tokens per second, 1.63 times higher, with a bit-identical loss curve (Figure 6).

Figure 6: Per-step communication volume: 10.87 GB with all_gather compared with 0.45 GB with all_to_all.

Communication cost. Newton–Schulz is only about 2 percent of the FLOPs in a training step (1.95 × 1014 of 9.53 × 1015), so communication was the bottleneck. Over NeuronLink-v3 at 1.28 TB/s, the 0.45 GB exchange takes under 0.4 ms of the roughly 4.4-second step.

Challenge 3: Backward-pass unrolling for a sequential recurrence

The backward pass differentiates through all 16 sequential state updates. On GPU, autograd builds this graph at runtime. On Trainium2, the compiler must see the whole unrolled 16-step graph in advance, which creates three constraints.

Graph depth grows with chunk count: at 32 chunks (C = 64), the graph overflowed the scheduler. Per-chunk memory grows with chunk size: at 8 chunks (C = 256), intermediates spilled into HBM. Every shape is fixed at trace time, so each loop intermediate needs its own static allocation.

Sixteen chunks (C = 128) satisfy all three: the unroll fits the scheduler, intermediates stay on chip, and tiles align with the 128 SBUF partitions.

Training results

The GenAIIC team trained Laplace 3B on one trn2.48xlarge instance using all 64 logical NeuronCores and the all_to_all Muon path. The full recipe is 190,735 steps (100 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens). The following results are through step 84,210, about 44 billion tokens.

Throughput. After compilation warmup, throughput settles at roughly 120,000 tokens per second and holds there through step 84,210.

Loss and gradient stability. The loss (Figure 7a) drops smoothly from about 11.4 to 2.3729 at step 84,210. The gradient norm (Figure 7b) shows the expected early spike then a steady decline to about 0.05, with no post-warmup spikes, divergence, or NaN/Inf values.

Figure 7: Training dynamics. (a) Loss 11.4 → 2.3729. (b) Gradient norm from TensorBoard data.

Inference optimization on Trainium2

Through an unmodified vLLM engine, the GenAIIC team served 11,544 output tokens per second at 1,280 concurrent sequences on one trn2.48xlarge instance.

Constant serving state. The 29.5 MB recurrent state per sequence is roughly 82 times smaller than a comparable KV cache at 8,192 tokens. Increasing the prompt from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens added only 0.5% to the cost per output token.

Unmodified vLLM. A wrapper replaces one attribute per decoder layer, the token mixer, to read and write the recurrent state in the vLLM pool. Because the model declares itself attention-free, vLLM allocates one fixed page per sequence. Outputs matched the i14 reference token for token (48/48 steps on 3/3 prompts in BF16).

Finding the bottleneck. A linear fit of decode time against the number of decoder layers L gives:


At L = 24, that is 168.1 ms per step, 96.9 percent of it inside the decoder layers. The large projections cost 13.27 ms, near the 12 ms HBM-streaming floor. Most time went to small operators dispatched one at a time under eager PyTorch.

Scaling to a full instance. Without tensor parallelism, throughput scales through replicas, with one engine and 20 sequences per logical NeuronCore. Eager throughput grew from 133 output tokens per second on one replica to 6,772 on 64, where host CPU usage reached 82 percent. Compiling the decode step removed per-operator dispatch and raised throughput 1.7 times, to 11,544 (Figure 8).

Figure 8: Whole-instance inference throughput. (a) Replica scaling on eager and compiled decode. (b) Compiled decode lifts throughput from 6,772 to 11,544 output tokens per second.

What fixed-batch benchmarks hide. Under real traffic, each new decode batch width is a separately compiled shape whose first use costs about 11 seconds. These steps were only 1.1 percent of the total but consumed 47.5 percent of decode time. Padding to fixed widths removed this cost with bit-exact results. Compiled decode then improved per-replica throughput 3.52 times under staggered arrivals, compared with 1.46 times on fixed batches. Because BF16 reassociation makes compiled output differ slightly from eager, use eager decode when exact reproducibility matters.

Key takeaways

The project produced lessons across both training and inference:

  • Native PyTorch can support custom architectures on Trainium2. i14 retained the GLA architecture and used TorchNeuron Native for the final implementation.
  • Communication design matters for custom optimizers. The Muon all_to_all design reduced per-rank traffic by 24 times and increased training throughput by 1.63 times.
  • Fixed state keeps inference memory predictable. Each sequence uses 29.5 MB regardless of context length.
  • Profile before compiling. Operator dispatch, rather than arithmetic or HBM bandwidth, accounted for most decode time.
  • Benchmark realistic arrival patterns. Fixed batches hid the cost of compiling new shapes for changing batch widths.

Conclusion

Laplace 3B shows that AWS Trainium2 can support model architectures beyond standard transformers. Using native PyTorch through TorchNeuron Native and the AWS Neuron SDK, i14 trained and served its GLA-based model while preserving a fixed recurrent state.

For agentic systems, this changes a basic serving constraint. Longer histories don’t require a larger per-sequence state, which can help teams retain more context while keeping memory use predictable.

If growing context is increasing serving cost, reducing concurrency, or limiting agent memory, try i14 or contact your AWS account team to evaluate Laplace 3B on AWS Trainium2.

Resources

  • Try i14
  • AWS Trainium and Trainium2
  • AWS Neuron SDK documentation
  • Native PyTorch support on AWS Trainium with TorchNeuron Native
  • Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training
  • Muon optimizer reference implementation
  • AWS Generative AI Innovation Center

 

About the authors

Kevin Shabahang

Kevin is VP of AI Research at i14, where he researches different model architectures. His work centers on applying insights from cognitive science and computational neuroscience to develop more efficient large language models.

Massimo Bardetti

Massimo is CTO of i14.ai, an AI research startup. He has led engineering teams at Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and startups in AI, neurotechnology, and entertainment. He also creates interactive art installations featured at festivals worldwide.

Iman Abbasnejad

Iman is an Applied Scientist at AWS, working with customers to design, develop, and deploy generative AI solutions. His work bridges AI research and practical applications, with a focus on large language models, agentic AI systems, model fine-tuning, and performance optimization to build reliable, efficient, and cost-effective AI solutions on AWS.

Xiaodong Yu

Xiaodong is a Machine Learning Engineer at AWS who focuses on generative AI, large language models, and machine learning performance optimization. His work covers efficient training and inference on AWS purpose-built machine learning accelerators, including AWS Trainium.

Daniel Wirjo

Daniel is a Solutions Architect at AWS focused on AI and SaaS startups. As a former startup CTO, he works with founders and engineering leaders to build and grow on AWS. Outside work, Daniel enjoys walking with a coffee, spending time in nature, and learning new ideas.

item.title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
item.dc:creator: Galina Jordanowa
item.description: The Smartsheet Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server lets AI agents read, update, and act on live work management data. This post shows two ways to connect it on AWS: Amazon Quick for business teams and Kiro for developers, so your agents can work with Smartsheet without switching tools.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet, the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.

With the Smartsheet MCP Server, AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language.

In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients.

Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.

The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right.

Figure 1: Smartsheet MCP Server architecture showing MCP client connections from Amazon Quick and Kiro through the server to the Smartsheet API layer

Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro

Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team:

When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard.

For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete.

Prerequisites

Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS.

Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place:

  • An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro)
  • A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan.
  • A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials if your client supports the OAuth flow.
  • For Amazon Quick: Author or higher permissions in your Amazon Quick account.
  • For Kiro: Kiro IDE installed from kiro.dev with Node.js available in your environment.

The Smartsheet MCP Server is available at three regional endpoints. It uses Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec versions 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26) and is authenticated with either OAuth 2.0 or a Personal Access Token.

  • Commercial US: https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
  • EU: https://mcp.smartsheet.eu.
  • AU: https://mcp.smartsheet.au.

Both options expose the same Smartsheet toolset. The right choice depends on where your work gets done:

Choose Amazon Quick if you need a fully managed, organization-wide solution your whole team can use: no app registration, only pre-built OAuth, and it scales across knowledge workers in your enterprise.

Choose Kiro if you’re a developer who wants something lightweight: no infrastructure, only a config file and a personal access token, scoped to your own workflow.

Amazon Quick integration

Amazon Quick includes Smartsheet as a pre-built connector in its directory. That means reading project status, updating rows, creating discussions, and surfacing risks, all in the same interface your business users already work in.

Amazon Quick makes that integration available across the organization, from project managers and operations teams to business users who manage work in Smartsheet.

To add the Quick integration:

  1. In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors and find Smartsheet in the directory.

Figure 2: The Smartsheet connector in the Amazon Quick Connectors directory

  1. Select the Smartsheet connector tile.
  2. Enter the following integration details:
    1. Name – Descriptive name for your Smartsheet integration.
    2. Keep the Connection type and Auth configuration settings as is.
    3. Base URL – https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
    4. Client ID – App client ID from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
    5. Client Secret – App secret from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
    6. Token URL – https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0/token.
    7. Auth URL – https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize.

Figure 3: Entering the Smartsheet connection details in Amazon Quick

  1. Choose Next.
  2. On the Manage Tools & Permissions page, you see a list of available tools. Choose Next.

Figure 4: The Manage Tools and Permissions page for the Smartsheet connector

  1. On the Publish page, choose who can access this connection, and then choose Publish.

Figure 5: Choosing who can access the Smartsheet connection on the Publish page

  1. Choose Next.

After you’re connected, your Amazon Quick chat agent can work with Smartsheet data through natural language:

  • “What projects in our portfolio are currently At Risk?”
  • “Update the status of the authentication task in the Backend API sheet to Complete.”
  • “Create a summary of all overdue items across the Q3 Roadmap and send it to the team.”

Figure 6: Amazon Quick chat response summarizing overdue tasks from a Smartsheet project sheet with key observations and recommended actions

Kiro integration

Kiro is the right path when developers want Smartsheet project context available directly in their development environment, alongside their code, without context-switching.

Kiro is built around spec-driven development. It turns high-level prompts into structured specs, then into working code, docs, and tests. MCP servers are how Kiro gets real-world context by connecting to documentation, databases, APIs, and enterprise systems to ground its agent in live data rather than training-time knowledge.

A Kiro feature called powers is a one-click installable bundle that packages a curated MCP server with steering files and hooks. It gives the Kiro coding agent a new capability out of the box. For Smartsheet, configuring the connection takes a single JSON configuration block and from that point, the Kiro agent can reference live project data as part of a development workflow.

To connect the Smartsheet MCP Server to Kiro, add it to your Kiro MCP configuration (.kiro/settings/mcp.json for workspace scope). For a full walkthrough, see Getting Started with Kiro and MCP Servers:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "smartsheet-us": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.smartsheet.com",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN>"
      }
    }
  }
}

This configuration uses the Personal Access Token (API key) approach. For production deployments, OAuth is recommended.

Set SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN to your Smartsheet Personal Access Token in your environment. Kiro loads MCP servers as background processes on startup. After it’s initialized, Smartsheet tools are available to the Kiro agent across all modes: chat, spec planning, and hooks-based automation. Full details in the Smartsheet MCP Server Documentation.

From there, Kiro can reference Smartsheet data as part of development workflows:

  • “Check the Backend API project sheet for any open bugs and generate a prioritized fix list.”

Figure 7: Kiro generating a prioritized fix list from open bugs in the Backend API project sheet

  • “Pull the Q3 Roadmap sheet and create a spec for the features marked In Progress.”

Figure 8: Kiro creating a spec from the in-progress features in the Q3 Roadmap sheet

Enterprise governance

For builders deploying in regulated or enterprise environments, the Smartsheet MCP Server security model is built on the same infrastructure and permissions layer as the Smartsheet REST API. It’s not a new trust boundary:

  • OAuth 2.0 and Personal Access Token authentication: choose the auth method supported by your MCP client.
  • User-level permission enforcement: agents can only access data the authenticated user has permission to see. No privilege escalation through natural language prompts.
  • Organization-level AI controls: system administrators can turn on or off AI features globally. Write-tool access is configurable by user group.
  • Streamable HTTP transport: firewall allowlisting is done by fully qualified domain name (FQDN) (mcp.smartsheet.com), not IP address.

For compliance architects, the MCP Server doesn’t store prompts, and prompt content stays between the AI client and the model. Smartsheet sees only the structured tool calls and their results.

Clean up

If you followed this walkthrough and want to remove the integration afterward, here’s how to undo each path:

Amazon Quick

  1. In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors.
  2. Select your Smartsheet connector.
  3. Choose Delete to remove the connection. This revokes the OAuth token and stops agent access to Smartsheet data.

Kiro

  1. Open your MCP configuration file (.kiro/settings/mcp.json).
  2. Remove the smartsheet-us entry from the mcpServers object.
  3. Restart Kiro to unload the server.

Next steps

For background on how the server works, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS. After you’ve connected the Smartsheet MCP Server to your system of choice, here are four actions we recommend trying:

You can ask the chat agent to monitor your active project sheets, identify rows marked Blocked or At Risk. You can also ask to annotate projects with a discussion comment, and deliver a structured summary to your team through your preferred channel. This would be an example workflow that chains get_sheet_summary, search, and create_discussion_on_row.

The agent can also retrieve data through the Smartsheet MCP Server to reconcile task statuses between your issue tracker and your Smartsheet project plan. It can flag drift between the two, and update the affected rows, using get_sheet_summary, get_columns, update_rows, and create_discussion_on_row in sequence.

You can also try to aggregate project health signals across your reports and dashboards. You can use it to produce a structured briefing without manual data gathering, drawing on list_reports, get_report, list_dashboards, get_dashboard, and search.

Lastly, you can use the agent to follow every write with a discussion comment explaining what changed and why. This creates a human-readable audit trail inside Smartsheet through the combination of update_rows and create_discussion_on_row.

All four patterns work across the preceding paths: Amazon Quick for business-user-facing workflows, and Kiro for developer-initiated actions.

Building something with Smartsheet MCP and AWS? Share what you’re working on in the comments, or connect with us in the Smartsheet Developer Community.

 

About the authors

Galina Jordanowa

Galina is a senior product marketing manager II at Smartsheet. She translates complex AI and product capabilities into clear, strategic market narratives and go-to-market (GTM) motions. She brings 26+ years in B2B SaaS marketing and a dev background that means she actually gets how builders think. Throughout her career, she’s connected technical depth with business impact and stays genuinely energized by what’s next in AI and the new ways it’s reshaping how teams build and work.

Pyone Thant Win

Pyone is a Partner Solutions Architect at AWS, where she supports strategic ISV partners to bring AI-powered solutions to market. She works at the intersection of cloud infrastructure and partner networks, helping partners use AWS services from AI/ML capabilities to data integration patterns to build deeper, more intelligent product experiences. Her work bridges hands-on technical partnership and go-to-market strategy, delivering joint solutions and industry offerings that reach shared customers.

Vishnu Elangovan

Vishnu is a Worldwide Agentic AI Solution Architect with over a decade of experience in Applied AI/ML and Deep Learning. He loves building and tinkering with scalable AI/ML solutions and considers himself a lifelong learner. Vishnu is a trusted thought leader in the AI/ML community, regularly speaking at leading AI conferences and sharing his expertise on Agentic AI at top-tier events.

item.title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Vineet Kachhawaha
item.description: Enterprise supply chains are data-rich but insight-poor, with the data to decide scattered across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email. This post shows how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore exposes those systems as a governed tool layer, and how Amazon Quick turns them into one conversational experience for business users, with a deploy-it-yourself walkthrough.
item.content:encoded:
Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions.

Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker.

Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited.

Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself.

The problem: Data-rich, insight-poor

Figure 1: Domain expertise sits with users while operational data is fragmented across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email

Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual.

A day in the life

A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches.

Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes.

Figure 2: Traditional multi-tool flow versus a single conversational thread orchestrated by AgentCore

Deep dive: Supply chain scenario walkthrough

The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation.

Step 1: Discovery – “What tools do I have?”

The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector.

Step 2: Querying – “Show me active disruptions”

“Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP (assess_disruption_impact): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export.

Step 3: Drill-down – “Assess the critical one”

The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002") correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP.

Step 4: Action – “Get mitigation recommendations”

The user asks for mitigation. recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002") chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs.

Step 5: Automated follow-up

The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”). The same flow can run unattended from an inbound supplier email. How we solve it: the same agent and tools run on a schedule or email trigger, posting review-ready cards to the Activity Feed for a person to approve.

Put end to end, those five steps are a single runtime sequence:

Figure 3: Runtime sequence for the walkthrough, where every result returns to Amazon Quick for approval

Solution architecture

That’s the experience. Here’s how it is built: the pattern separates the intelligence layer from the interface layer, so each evolves independently, with Amazon Quick as the interface and AgentCore as the intelligence.

Figure 4: End-to-end architecture from Amazon Quick to AgentCore (Gateways, Runtime, Identity, Policy) to backends, with AWS Agent Registry alongside

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: The intelligence layer

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a modular agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale. It offers more than we use here. Four of its services are relevant to this pattern:

  • Runtime – Serverless hosting for MCP servers and agents, with session isolation and built-in identity.
  • Gateway – Turns APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and services into MCP-compatible tools behind a secure managed endpoint, standardizing tool access. Reasoning is the calling agent’s.
  • Identity – Authentication and credential management, compatible with existing identity providers.
  • Policy – Deterministic authorization rules, authored in natural language or Cedar, that intercept every tool call before execution, keeping an agent in its lane on procurement and financial data.

The MCP protocol: How tools communicate

MCP is an open standard for how AI models interact with external tools. Each server exposes tools with typed parameters:

{
  "server_name": "sc-disruption-alert-gateway",
  "tools": [{
    "name": "assess_disruption_impact",
    "parameters": {
      "disruption_id": {"type": "string"},
      "context": {"type": "object"} // order, inventory, revenue data
    }
  }] // plus classify_severity, recommend_mitigation, get_escalation_chain
}

This means:

  • AI clients (Quick, custom agents, other MCP apps) can consume the same servers.
  • Backends (SAP, Oracle, custom microservices) can be wrapped as an MCP server.
  • Tool discovery is automatic. Clients query the registry for schemas at runtime.

AWS Agent Registry: The discovery layer

The registry is the governed discovery layer: a publisher submits a record, a curator approves it, and only then is it discoverable through hybrid search, browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint. One scale reality worth noting: because schemas are discovered at runtime, treat each as a contract, versioning new alongside old for breaking changes.

Figure 5: Publishing an MCP server record to AWS Agent Registry, a curator approving it, an administrator linking it to Quick, and approved records becoming connector cards

Multi-step orchestration

The reasoning layer is an agent on AgentCore Runtime, an agent record at its direct invocation URL through a Custom MCP connector, with no Lambda or gateway. Here, it’s the Order Fulfillment Agent. Given one request it plans which tools to call and in what order:

User: "A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, issue an emergency RFQ."
Disruption Alerts MCP -> identify the disruption
Governance MCP -> approved alternatives + compliance + budget authority
Quoting MCP -> contract-aligned quote
-> one consolidated recommendation

Security and governance architecture

Every tool call passes through the same AgentCore control set before it reaches a backend.

Figure 6: The uniform AgentCore control set before the backend (IAM auth, per-tool authorization, input validation, policy evaluation, rate limiting, data-boundary enforcement, audit logging)

The MCP servers in this pattern

MCP server Capabilities Example queries
Quoting Engine (sc-quoting-gateway) Quote generation, pricing rules, validation “Contract-aligned quote for 500 units of SKU-A”
Governance Engine (sc-governance-gateway) Supplier approval, budget authority, regulatory compliance, policy rules “Is SupplierCo on our approved vendor list?”
Invoice Processing (sc-invoice-gateway) Invoice approval routing, AP aging, payment schedules “What invoices are pending approval this week?”
Disruption Alerts (sc-disruption-alert-gateway) Active disruptions, severity, impact assessments, mitigation “Critical disruptions affecting our APAC suppliers?”
Order Fulfillment Agent (sc-order-fulfillment-agent) Multi-step orchestration across all four business MCPs (AgentCore Runtime, direct invocation URL) “A supplier went down, find alternatives, check compliance, issue an RFQ”

Amazon Quick: The enterprise AI assistant

Amazon Quick puts AgentCore tools before business users through chat, agents, the Activity Feed, and automated workflows, with no technical setup.

Key components used

Component Role in this pattern How it works
Agent Registry connection Surfaces MCP servers as connectors Admin links the registry once. Records become connector cards
Quick Agent One SC agent that adapts to role Tailors to persona (manager, procurement, analyst)
MCP connectors Expose MCP tools in chat A card connector exposes tools across Chat, agents, schedules
Activity Feed Proactive alerts and actions Agents post cards. The user acts
Schedules Recurring natural-language automation For example, “every morning”
Outlook Integration Email into the feed Supplier replies parsed and validated
Structured data connectors Query operational records Quick queries Space datasets (orders, inventory, suppliers, contracts) for the MCP rule check
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) knowledge base Retrieval over documents Invoices, contracts, policies in an S3 knowledge base, grounding answers through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
CRM connector (optional) Reads customer records (optional) CRM (for example, Salesforce) accounts, opportunities, contacts. Can also load into datasets

Automated Activity Feed and proactive monitoring

The Activity Feed is the proactive surface of Amazon Quick, a unified inbox where agents post results, alerts, and recommendations. Feed items are:

  • Actionable, each carries context and next-step actions.
  • AI-triaged, with priority indicators (Reply needed, Follow up, Deadline).
  • Cross-source, spanning email, schedules, agent runs, and external systems.
  • Human-in-the-loop, where agents propose and humans decide.

How automated monitoring works

AgentCore tools plus the proactive capabilities of Amazon Quick give two paths, time-based and email-driven, through a common trigger → agent → output pipeline.

Figure 7: Three-stage pipeline from trigger (schedule or email) to autonomous agent (assess_disruption_impact, check_supplier_approval, apply_approval_rules, validate_quote) to review-ready card

Use case: Validate supplier responses from email

Suppliers reply to an emergency RFQ by email with pricing. The agent validates each (approved supplier? within guidelines?) and stages the result. It does not author a quote, pick a winner, or issue a purchase order (PO).

Phase 1: Setup (one-time, approximately 5 minutes)

  1. Connect Outlook: in Amazon Quick, choose Settings → Connections → Add Outlook.
  2. Configure Activity Feed: turn on email monitoring in feed preferences.
  3. Create SC Agent: build an agent with these instructions:
Supply chain procurement assistant. On a supplier RFQ reply with pricing: 1) extract SKU(s), quantities, pricing; 2) validate approved vendor (Governance MCP); 3) check pricing within guidelines (Quoting MCP); 4) post a review-ready card (approved-supplier, within-guidelines); do NOT draft a PO or select a supplier.
  1. Create Schedule: “Every 2 hours during business hours, check for new supplier replies and validate them.”

Phase 2: Runtime (fully automated)

Schedule -> email from "TechSupply Co" (MCU-7200, 10,000 units @ $2.45/unit) -> Governance MCP: approved? | Quoting MCP: within guidelines? -> "Supplier Response - Ready for Review" card

The feed card carries the validation results and decision-relevant facts:

Supplier Response: Ready for Review Details
Supplier TechSupply Co, approved vendor
SKU / Qty / Price MCU-7200 · 10,000 units · $2.45/unit
Price check within purchasing guidelines
Actions Select for PO · Compare responses · Reject

Phase 3: Human-in-the-loop

The reviewer compares validated responses and either selects a supplier and issues the PO, or rejects with a logged reason. Selection and the PO stay with a person.

Use case: Proactive disruption monitoring

Schedule-triggered, the same pattern applies: a daily 8:30 AM agent checks for new critical or high-severity disruptions, assesses impact, flags anything under seven days of supply as URGENT, and posts an alert card with an Issue Emergency RFQ action.

Where this fits alongside traditional BI

Dimension Traditional business intelligence (BI) / dashboards AgentCore + Amazon Quick
Access model Navigate, log in, find the dashboard/report Ask in natural language. The system finds the source
Time to insight Minutes to hours (find → filter → export → correlate) Seconds (ask → answer with cross-system context)
Multi-system correlation Manual: 3-4 tabs, copy-paste Automatic: the agent orchestrates across MCP servers from one query
Action gap Insight in one tool → switch → act in another Insight → action in the same conversation
Setup cost Weeks/months (dashboard design, ETL, permissions, training) Minutes to connect, once your MCP servers exist
Run cost Fixed: pipelines cost the same whether or not anyone asks Usage-based: serverless scales to zero, cost tracks questions (Lambda + agent tokens)
Trust & accuracy As fresh as the last ETL load Computed live from systems of record and grounded docs, every write human-gated

This isn’t a “replace everything” argument. Dashboards remain superior for trend visualization, collaborative analysis, regulatory reporting, and exploratory analysis. Use conversational AI for real-time operational decisions and BI for strategic analysis. They complement, not compete.

Personas and use cases

One Quick Agent serves all three personas: the manager maintains continuity, procurement sources with compliance-awareness, the analyst correlates signals. Persona also bounds reach, through row/column-level security and per-persona MCP-tool scoping, so procurement does not see finance data.

Persona Use case Tools invoked Outcome
SC Manager Morning disruption check Disruption Alerts MCP Disruptions, revenue at risk, days of supply
SC Manager Emergency procurement Governance → Quoting MCP Verified alternatives + RFQ, one flow
Procurement Supplier verification, budget authority Governance MCP Approval, compliance, limits
Procurement RFQ generation and response validation Quoting MCP RFQ issued + responses validated
Ops Analyst Cross-system correlation SC Operations Agent Multi-MCP reasoning, one query
Ops Analyst Payment queue, audit, disruption trends Invoice / Governance MCP AP aging, audit log, patterns

Getting started

Deploying the pattern takes three phases: provision the infrastructure, connect Amazon Quick to your data and the registry, and turn on monitoring.

Prerequisites

Before you begin:

  • An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS Agent Registry.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) CLI, and Docker (the agent runs as an arm64 container).
  • Python 3.12 or later, with Boto3 1.43.94 or later for the registry step.
  • Active credentials with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to deploy and register (aws sts get-caller-identity returns the target account).
  • Data layer: a database (Snowflake, PostgreSQL/RDS, or a SQLAlchemy engine), an Amazon S3 bucket, optionally a Salesforce org.
  • Amazon Quick set up for your organization.
  • (Optional) An Outlook account for email automation.

Setup uses two surfaces, so each of the following steps names where it happens: the Amazon Quick web console in a browser (Amazon Quick Sight permissions, Agent Registry linking, connectors, and agent settings) and the Quick Desktop App (connecting Outlook for email automation). The conversational experience in the Desktop App comes last, once setup is done.

Deploy the infrastructure

Everything is open source and scripted: clone the quick-for-supply-chain example in the aws-samples/sample-amazon-quick-suite-knowledge-hub repository and follow its README.md, or point a coding agent like Kiro at it.

The README.md covers three phases. Phase 1 deploys the AgentCore stack: the identity layer (an Amazon Cognito user pool and app client, authorization-code OAuth flow, plus a test user), four business-rule MCP servers (each an AWS Lambda function fronted by its own AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using CUSTOM_JWT authorization), the gateway targets mapping the tools of each Lambda function, and sc-order-fulfillment-agent on AgentCore Runtime as a container, with least-privilege IAM roles. Phase 2 uploads the synthetic dataset to Amazon S3. Phase 3 verifies gateways and runtime are Ready. Six Agent Registry records are approved.

Figure 8: AWS Agent Registry console with six approved records (four MCP Server, one Agent, one Skills)

Grant Amazon Quick access to your data

In the Amazon Quick web console (browser): grant Amazon Quick access from the Amazon Quick Sight admin page (Manage Quick Sight → Security and permissions) to both the S3 bucket and Amazon Athena, since each table is served through an Athena source over an AWS Glue database. Without the Athena grant, dataset creation fails.

Figure 9: Amazon Quick Sight Security and permissions, with Amazon Athena alongside Amazon S3

Link the registry and create connectors

Linking the registry is one-time and administrator-level. Creating a connector is per-user. Both happen in the Amazon Quick console. See the AWS Agent Registry integration guide.

Link the registry (administrator, one-time)

An administrator links one Agent Registry to the Quick account. In the Amazon Quick web console (admin): go to Manage account → Permissions → AWS Agent Registry and turn on the registry (sc-supply-chain-registry, one per account). Only registries in your account and Region, agent-registry namespace, AWS_IAM (SigV4) authorization, and READY status appear. The Quick-managed service role links it.

Figure 10: Linking the registry, where only READY, AWS_IAM registries are selectable

Create a connector

After the registry is linked, approved MCP server records become connector cards: the four business MCPs as cards, the order-fulfillment agent added manually. At scale, federate connector authentication through your identity provider and provision connectors to groups, with the Cognito user pool as the seam.

In the Amazon Quick web console (per user): the four cards appear on the Connectors page (sc-quoting-mcp, sc-governance-mcp, sc-invoice-processing-mcp, sc-disruption-alert-mcp). Authenticate through the OAuth authorization-code flow (OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE) with client ID, secret, and token, authorization, and redirect URLs from the deploy script. Sign in as the test user, turn on tools, create and share.

Figure 11: The four business-MCP connector cards, with the order-fulfillment agent added manually

Registry-sourced connectors are Custom MCP connectors (relevant for custom permissions). Removing the link later doesn’t delete connectors already created.

Figure 12: The Authenticate step using the authorization-code OAuth flow (OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE)

Add the order-fulfillment agent connector

In the Amazon Quick web console: because it is an agent record, create its connector manually (Connectors → Create for your team → Model Context Protocol → Create new): name it sc-order-fulfillment-agent, point it at the AgentCore Runtime direct invocation URL from the deploy script, complete the same OAuth sign-in, create and share.

Figure 13: Creating the sc-order-fulfillment-agent connector, pointed at the AgentCore runtime invocation URL

Attach the connectors to your agent

The deployment creates the Supply Chain agent: a Quick Space, imported datasets and S3 knowledge base, and the agent with instructions, starter prompts, and welcome message. What remains is attaching the connectors.

In the Amazon Quick web console (agent settings): open the deployment-created Supply Chain agent (default id sc-supply-chain-agent) and attach all five connectors (four business MCPs plus sc-order-fulfillment-agent), or pass the five connector IDs to the setup script.

Set up proactive monitoring

To make it proactive, Quick runs the same agent on a schedule or on incoming email and posts results to the Activity Feed. Both paths reuse the agent and tools you configured.

In the Quick Desktop App (Settings → Connections): connect Outlook and turn on email monitoring. Then, in Quick Chat, create two natural-language schedules, time-based (“Every morning, check for new critical disruptions”) and email-driven (“Every two hours in business hours, check supplier replies and validate”). The agent extracts pricing, runs the checks, and posts a card.

Try it in Amazon Quick

With the agent and connectors ready, ask in natural language in Amazon Quick Chat. Each prompt shows the data-then-rules pattern.

Ask Amazon Quick What you get
“What supply chain tools do I have?” The five MCP connectors (quoting, governance, invoice, disruption alerts, order-fulfillment agent), with status.
“Show me active supply disruptions.” Active disruptions with severity, region, SKU counts (Disruption Alerts MCP).
“Assess the impact of the TechComp production halt.” Revenue at risk, affected orders, days of supply, from your datasets.
“Is this supplier an approved vendor, and do we have budget authority for a $72,000 PO?” An approval from the Governance MCP (vendor status, budget authority, compliance).
“Generate a contract-aligned quote for 1,000 units for this customer.” A contract-aligned quote from the Quoting MCP, as a branded document.
“A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, and issue an emergency RFQ.” The Order Fulfillment Agent chains disruption, governance, and quoting MCPs into one recommendation.

Conclusion

AgentCore and Amazon Quick are a repeatable enterprise-AI pattern: separate intelligence from interface. AgentCore turns fragmented backends into a composable, governed, AI-accessible layer through standard MCP interfaces. Amazon Quick democratizes access in natural language.

The gain is the collapsed decision chain: detect, research, decide, act, and log once spanned five tools, now one conversation. The AI researches, correlates, validates. The person decides. Every call is authenticated, authorized, policy-checked, and audited, and a 45-60 minute routine across five systems can collapse to minutes.

That is the shift from data-rich, insight-poor to data-rich, decision-ready. Start with one MCP server and one persona. The registry grows and the experience stays the same.

About the authors

Vineet Kachhawaha

Vineet is a Sr. Worldwide Agentic AI Solution Architect at AWS, focused on Amazon Quick. He works closely with enterprise customers and partners to design, deploy, and scale AI-driven solutions. Vineet also co-led the AWS for Legal Tech initiative, helping legal and compliance organizations harness AI/ML to drive business value. He loves building and tinkering with agentic AI solutions and considers himself a lifelong learner. Vineet regularly speaks at AWS events and industry conferences, sharing his expertise on generative AI and agentic architectures.

Kamlesh Mariwala

Kamlesh is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at Amazon Web Services (AWS), focused on the automotive and manufacturing industries. He helps customers design scalable, secure, and cost-effective architectures that use generative AI, agentic AI, and machine learning to solve complex business problems and speed up time to value.

Sachin Sathaye

Sachin is a Head of Data and AI GTM and Architectures at AWS, where he advises enterprise leaders on their data and AI transformations. He partners with CXOs to design, deploy, and scale AI-driven solutions that turn strategy into measurable business value, with focus on supply chain, commercial excellence, new product introduction, manufacturing operations, and enterprise business services. Sachin is the author of “The 12 Factors of Enterprise Agentic AI: A Value Chain,” a vendor-agnostic framework for building production-grade agentic systems, and a recognized voice on operationalizing generative and agentic AI at scale.

item.title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
item.dc:creator: Mijanur Palash
item.description: Learn how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with GRPO. SFT took reasoning-language accuracy from 22% to 100%, and GRPO added measurable gains where headroom existed.
item.content:encoded:
GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent).

For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both?

In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome.

Solution overview

This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod.

The task and dataset

The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT).

Two metrics matter:

  • Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language?
  • Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language?

How SFT and GRPO fit together

The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post.

The training stack

We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO.

The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre.

Figure 1: End-to-end training data path for SFT and GRPO fine-tuning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with veRL, Ray, KubeRay, vLLM, and Amazon FSx for Lustre for Qwen control experiments

The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints. When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with Amazon EKS orchestration. GPT-OSS SFT used 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB). The Qwen control used 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S).
  • An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system mounted on the cluster with a PersistentVolumeClaim named fsx-claim at /fsx.
  • EFA-enabled instances and a working NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and aws-ofi-nccl stack for multi-node SFT.
  • A container registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to hold the training image built from the reference repository.
  • A HuggingFace access token for openai/gpt-oss-20b and the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), kubectl, docker, and envsubst available on your workstation.

Set up the training environment

All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/. Clone the repository and change into the test case directory:

git clone https://github.com/awslabs/awsome-distributed-ai
cd awsome-distributed-ai/3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo

Copy the environment template, then edit env_vars to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token:

cp env_vars.example env_vars
source env_vars

Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts:

cd artifacts && ./build_push.sh && cd ..

Point kubectl at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection:

aws eks update-kubeconfig --name <YOUR_CLUSTER_NAME> --region us-east-2
envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/fsx-storage-manager.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B with SFT and LoRA

We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results.

The base-model gap

Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction.

SFT configuration

The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic HyperPodPyTorchJob managed by Kueue, launched with hyperpodrun.

Apply the SFT manifest:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < hyperpod-eks/train-lora-hyperpod-elastic-g6e.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Watch training progress:

kubectl get pods -l app=gpt-oss-lora-elastic
kubectl logs -f -l app=gpt-oss-lora-elastic

Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this:

{'loss': 1.035, 'grad_norm': 0.163, 'learning_rate': 0.0002, 'mean_token_accuracy': 0.716, 'epoch': 3.25}
{'loss': 1.003, 'grad_norm': 0.171, 'lr': 0.0002, 'acc': 0.722, 'epoch': 3.32}
{'loss': 0.976, 'grad_norm': 0.159, 'lr': 0.0002, 'acc': 0.726, 'epoch': 3.57}

When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect:

kubectl exec -it fsx-storage-manager -- python /app/convert_fsdp_checkpoint.py \
  --checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/checkpoint-1000 \
  --output    /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/lora-checkpoint-1000-peft

SFT results and the staged learning curve

After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages:

  • Around step 200, the model learned to reason in the target language (reasoning-language metric hits 100 percent).
  • Around step 1000, the model additionally learned to give the answer in the target language.

Final SFT eval (step 1000):

  • Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (50/50).
  • Answer-language correct: 62 percent (31/50).
  • Both correct: 62 percent (31/50).
  • Per-language answer accuracy: FR 60 percent, DE 60 percent, ES 30 percent, IT 60 percent, EN 100 percent.

Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there.

Refine answer-language with GRPO

Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce.

Run GRPO on top of the SFT checkpoint

We ran GRPO with TRL’s GRPOTrainer, starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call merge_and_unload, and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, device_map=auto, learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0.

Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/train-grpo-singlenode.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl logs -f grpo-single

GRPO writes checkpoints to /fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/. Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation.

Result (from the SFT checkpoint):

  • Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (held: GRPO didn’t break what SFT taught).
  • Answer-language correct: 62 to 70 percent (+8 points, 35/50).
  • Both correct: 70 percent.
  • Per-language answer: FR 70 percent, DE 80 percent, ES 60 percent, IT 40 percent, EN 100 percent.

GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it.

Compare base, SFT, and GRPO inference side by side

To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/inference-g6e-base.yaml    | kubectl apply -f -
envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/inference-g6e-trained.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/inference-g6e-grpo.yaml    | kubectl apply -f -

Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant:

kubectl exec -it inference-base    -- python /app/inference_g6e.py \
  --reasoning_language French

kubectl exec -it inference-trained -- python /app/inference_g6e.py \
  --checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/lora-checkpoint-1000-peft \
  --reasoning_language French

kubectl exec -it inference-grpo    -- python /app/inference_grpo_new.py \
  --use_grpo \
  --grpo_checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/checkpoint-1470-peft \
  --reasoning_language French

The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English. The GRPO pod reasons and answers in French. To reproduce the full 50-case eval that generated the numbers earlier, run the evaluation manifest and read the result file from the FSx storage manager:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/eval-grpo.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl logs -f eval-grpo
kubectl exec fsx-storage-manager -- \
  cat /fsx/experiments/grpo_eval_checkpoint1470_*.txt

To understand more broadly when GRPO adds value, we ran a controlled experiment on Qwen2.5-7B across two tasks with different capability gaps.

Test the pattern with a Qwen2.5-7B control

To test the “match technique to capability gap” thesis on a different model and different tasks, we ran controlled experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The first task is the same multilingual reasoning task (where headroom exists). The second task is GSM8K, where the model is already at peak accuracy. This is an internal experiment, and the public repo has not yet been released.

Infrastructure: 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S), EFA 100Gbps, FSx Lustre, Ray 2.44 + KubeRay 1.4.2, veRL v0.6.1, vLLM 0.8.4.

Arms: A = base, B = SFT-only, C = SFT+GRPO.

Multilingual reasoning (50 cases)

Metric A base B SFT C SFT+GRPO Δ GRPO
Structured format 0% 92% 98% +6
Reasoning language 0% 96% 98% +2
Answer language 0% 38% 44% +6
Both correct 0% 38% 44% +6

GSM8K, a task with no headroom

On GSM8K, base Qwen2.5-7B already scores 90.5 percent (181/200). GRPO at step 30 also scores 90.5 percent. When most sampled groups are all-correct, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, so there is no learning signal. This is the other half of the thesis: GRPO needs headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) to have anything to optimize. No headroom means no gain.

Best practices

  1. Start with SFT. GRPO cannot teach a behavior with zero base probability. It can only reinforce responses the model already sometimes produces. SFT took reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent, and every GRPO win in this work was built on that SFT checkpoint.
  2. Use LoRA for both SFT and GRPO. LoRA r=8/α=16 was parameter-efficient (0.068 percent trainable), and on the Qwen control it stayed numerically stable through GRPO (grad norm 0.23, about 11.7 GB per GPU). It’s a strong default when you want SFT and GRPO to share the same adapter shape.
  3. Match the technique to the gap. Use SFT for missing behavior. Use GRPO for refining an existing, sometimes-correct behavior. GRPO’s realistic ceiling here was +6 to +8 points.
  4. Check for reward headroom before spending GPU-hours. If most groups are all-correct (GSM8K 90.5 percent base), the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and GRPO gets no gradient. Verify there is headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) before starting a GRPO run.

Clean up resources

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the workload resources and then the underlying infrastructure:

  1. Delete the training and inference pods and jobs: 
    kubectl delete hyperpodpytorchjob lora-hyperpod-elastic --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete pod grpo-single inference-base inference-trained inference-grpo \
  eval-grpo fsx-storage-manager --ignore-not-found
  2. Scale down or delete the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster or its node groups.
  3. Delete the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system once you have exported any checkpoints you want to keep.
  4. Delete any Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets or objects used for training data or checkpoint archives.

Conclusion

We showed how to fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between SFT and GRPO. SFT did most of the work: reasoning-language went from 22 percent to 100 percent. GRPO added a real, modest refinement on top (answer 62 percent to 70 percent) where headroom existed. A parallel Qwen2.5-7B control confirmed the pattern. GRPO added +6 percent on multilingual reasoning, where there was room to improve. It added no gain on GSM8K, where the model was already at peak accuracy (90.5 percent).

Decision framework:

  • Behavior the model can’t do at all: use SFT.
  • Behavior it does sometimes, with headroom: use SFT then GRPO for a few points more.
  • Model already at peak accuracy, or target has zero base probability: GRPO won’t help.

To try this yourself, walk through the test cases in the awsome-distributed-ai repository. For more on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the service detail page and the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation. For a walkthrough of Ray on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the related post Running distributed training on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Ray and Amazon SageMaker Studio. The link will be added after that post is published. Share your results in the comments.

 

About the authors

Mijanur Palash

Mijanur is a Specialist Solutions Architect on the AI/ML Infrastructure team at AWS. He focuses on distributed training and reinforcement learning workloads on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod for automotive, pharmaceutical, and generative AI customers. Outside of work, Palash enjoys hiking and photography.

Mark Vinciguerra

Mark was a Worldwide Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at AWS, focused on distributed training and inference on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. He works with strategic customers on large-scale foundation-model workloads across EKS and Slurm orchestration and contributes reference architectures and workshops for HyperPod, Ray, and SageMaker Unified Studio.

item.title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
item.dc:creator: Urvish Saraiya
item.description: Octave built a secure, multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock, using Cohere Embed v4 for embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for isolated agent execution, to power a Complaint Triage Assistant that searches 2 billion regulated documents without crossing tenant boundaries.
item.content:encoded:
In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit.

Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500. Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance, supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary.

Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production.

Why a foundation, not a feature
