name:          [Large Orders]
description:   Purchases whose net line amount exceeds $500.
               Referenced by Large Order Spend and any metric that
               scopes to high-value transactions.
qualification: Purchase Amount > 500
permissions:   read:   Everyone
               modify: Data Modelers

Then reference the filters in metric expressions. Each of these is an advanced metric: a base aggregation qualified by a named filter.

Large Order Spend    Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} <[Large Orders]>
Sports Spend         Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} <[Sports Category]>
Rewards Spend        Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} <[Rewards Members]>

Figure 5 shows the Design Center view of an advanced metric with a filter condition applied. It uses the same authoring pattern as the preceding Large Order Spend.

Figure 5: Advanced-metric authoring in Design Center, showing the base formula and the filter condition referenced from the Large Orders filter object.

Customer Lifetime Spend also needs a level qualifier, because lifetime means the whole history regardless of how the current question is sliced:

Customer Lifetime Spend    Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+, !Customer+}

The ! before Customer sets grouping to none, so the metric returns each customer’s full total on every row rather than collapsing to one row per customer. See Strategy Metric Level Symbols for the full syntax.

Notice that [Big Spender] in the filter table qualifies on a metric expression rather than an attribute predicate. Filter objects can gate on either. Share of wallet is a compound metric, built from other metrics:

Sports Share of Wallet    [Sports Spend] / [Customer Lifetime Spend]

Levels and conditions carry through from the components unchanged. Share of wallet is a ratio, so it doesn’t add or average. The share across an AWS Region isn’t the average of each customer’s share, and the metric description tells the agent that. See Strategy Conditional Metrics.

Beyond base, advanced, and compound, Mosaic ships governed time-intelligence metrics as first-class expressions. Previous Year, Previous Quarter, Year-to-Date, and Quarter-to-Date are declared once on the model and preserved through slice, so a question like how does Sports spend this year compare with last year becomes an attribute pick and two metric references rather than a hand-written SQL date filter. Custom calendars attach at the model level, so the same year-over-year expression works for a fiscal year that ends in September and a calendar year that ends in December. See Governed Time-Intelligence Metrics in Mosaic.

Edit the filter object once and the Power BI dashboard, the SQL extract, and the agent all move together. That is what a named, governed model artifact gets you that an inline SQL predicate cannot.

How Mosaic plans and executes queries

The Mosaic engine parses each MCP query call as Trino-dialect SQL, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying Purchase and Customer models, applies the RLS or OLS that the caller is subject to, and plans physical SQL per source. The dialect matches what Strategy publishes for the MCP query tool, so the SQL the agent emits is portable across MCP clients connecting to the same certified model.

For the auto-enrollment question, planning unfolds like this:

  1. Push down to Amazon Aurora: a join of customer and rewards_account on cid, projecting profile and rewards_account.create_date, filtered where enrollment is null. Returns one row per unenrolled customer.
  2. Push down to Amazon Redshift: SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid. Returns one row per customer with total spend.
  3. Combine inside Mosaic: join the two intermediate result sets on cid (the linking attribute), rank by lifetime spend, and return the top 20.

Aurora runs a transactional profile join. Amazon Redshift runs the fact aggregation. Mosaic handles the cross-engine join on a small intermediate set (one row per customer, not one row per order). A hand-written pipeline approximates the same shape and then must be kept in sync forever.

One SQL detail matters. Metrics are governed values, but Trino treats them as selected columns, so when a query uses GROUP BY, metrics need an aggregation wrapper such as SUM(metric_name). The metric’s definition, conditions, and join paths are still resolved by Mosaic. The outer aggregation is the caller’s. A non-additive ratio like share of wallet therefore needs to say so in its description.

Live pushdown or in-memory

Every Mosaic model runs in one of two modes.

Mode Behavior Best fit
Live Pushdown to Redshift or Aurora at query time Consistently-current data. Source security applies directly
In-memory Answered from a Mosaic-resident cube Bounded recent windows. Predictable latency. No per-query warehouse compute

Both modes enforce the same security rules. RLS and OLS are set once on the model and evaluated regardless of where the answer comes from. The choice is a performance and cost question.

Agent traffic is repetitive and bursty. An agent decomposing top spenders in Wisconsin into several exploratory follow-ups fires many small queries over the same recent slice. Serving that from memory turns variable per-query warehouse spend into fixed Mosaic capacity, and it’s usually faster. For interactive agent workloads over a bounded window, in-memory is often both quicker and cheaper. Configure Mosaic-side entitlements before switching a model to in-memory, and validate them in the same test pass you use to validate the numbers.

One definition, four interfaces

The metrics, attributes, hierarchies, and security rules built in the previous section reach every consumer through native protocols. No connector translation, no metric re-implementation, no drift.

Protocol Typical consumer What it uses Mosaic for
MCP AI agents (Strands, Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini) Semantic discovery + governed query
SQL / JDBC / ODBC (Trino) Tableau, SQL clients, Python notebooks Flexibility and ad-hoc analysis
DAX / XMLA Power BI, Excel PivotTables Semantic fidelity for BI
REST Custom applications, data science Programmatic access

The same certified Mosaic model that the Strands agent in this walkthrough consumes also serves a business analyst working in Amazon Quick, which registers Mosaic MCP as an OAuth-authenticated connector. No second integration is required.

Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement

Mosaic enforces access in the semantic layer, before a query reaches Amazon Redshift or Aurora. HR and fraud roles see personally identifiable information (PII) fields like ssn and card_num. Marketing and analytics roles do not. Enforcement is identical whether the caller is a Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One set of RLS and OLS objects, one certified-model gate, one privilege check. Attributes and metrics marked as sensitive also feed Mosaic Sentinel Risk Management, which alerts on queries that touch flagged objects and detects behavioral anomalies as a defense-in-depth layer next to OLS.

Figure 6 shows the identity propagation chain across two lanes: the front-door OAuth handshake that runs once per user, and the per-request path that runs on every agent tool call. Each lane carries the user’s identity end-to-end so Mosaic can enforce RLS and OLS on the caller rather than a service account.

Figure 6: Identity propagation chain. The front-door OAuth handshake runs once per user, or on refresh-token renewal (steps 1-4). The per-request path runs on every agent tool call (steps 5-10). Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Mosaic evaluates governance on the caller’s Strategy user identity.

The chain follows two lanes.

Front-door OAuth handshake (once per user). The human user authenticates against the enterprise IdP. The application starts an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow against Strategy Library at /collaboration/authorize with scope offline_access. Strategy Library, federated to the same IdP through SAML or OIDC, returns a refresh and access token pair at /collaboration/token. The app persists the refresh token to AWS Secrets Manager, keyed by the user’s IdP sub claim.

Per-request path (every agent tool call). AgentCore Gateway validates the IdP JWT and routes to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent invoking Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. The agent’s MCP tool retrieves the user’s refresh token from Secrets Manager, exchanges it for a fresh access token, and presents Authorization: Bearer <access_token> to /collaboration/mcp/mosaic. Mosaic resolves the token to a Strategy user, enforces the Use MCP Server privilege, certified-model gate, and RLS and OLS, then plans and executes against Purchase and Customer. A marketing analyst doesn’t see ssn or card_num. A fraud analyst does.

Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Governance evaluates on the caller’s identity from IdP to Mosaic engine.

Expose the layer through the Mosaic MCP server

Strategy Library exposes two MCP endpoints:

Endpoint Path What it does
Agents MCP /collaboration/mcp/agent Routes a question to a certified Strategy agent, which answers using its own data and instructions
Mosaic MCP /collaboration/mcp/mosaic Queries Mosaic models and AI-enabled cubes directly, no Strategy agent required

Both work independently. This walkthrough uses Mosaic MCP. Putting the semantic layer directly in front of the Strands agent skips an inference hop.

The tool chain

Four tools, chained from project to model to semantics to query.

Tool What it does Parameters
get_projects Lists Strategy projects the caller can access none
get_models Lists certified Mosaic models and datasets in a project project
get_semantics Returns a model’s full definition: attributes and metrics with data types, descriptions, and metric formulas model
query Runs a read-only Trino SQL query. Writes and DDL rejected with MOSAIC_SQL_WRITE_REJECTED sql

The agent chains these calls automatically. get_projects and get_models narrow to the right model by description before the agent reads a column name. get_semantics returns the governed definitions the agent then uses to compose SQL against real object names: Sports Share of Wallet as a compound metric, Customer Lifetime Spend scoped to Customer, the Category hierarchy, and the formula for every metric.

Two Mosaic-specific SQL conventions matter. Column identifiers follow a <form>__<name> pattern and must be wrapped in double quotes ("customer__customer name"). Time attributes are exposed both as base columns and as pre-bucketed interval columns ((day interval), (month interval)), and the docs explicitly say to use the interval columns for time-grouped aggregations rather than date_trunc.

Metadata is what makes it accurate

get_semantics returns definitions, but the agent still must choose the right metric. Without descriptions, Total Spend and Customer Lifetime Spend look interchangeable, and they aren’t. Four properties do most of the work: object descriptions (what the metric means and when not to use it, including aggregation behavior for non-additive metrics), semantic definitions (how compound metrics compose), relationships (which attributes are valid slices), and governance context (so the agent can say what it can’t see rather than presenting a filtered number as complete). The model description is the first thing get_models returns and it’s how the agent picks the right model. Mosaic can import metadata from upstream catalogs, so column descriptions already maintained flow in rather than being retyped.

Deploy the agent

Strands is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the Mosaic MCP endpoint as a tool source. The AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and forwards the human user’s JWT.

The system prompt matters. Give the agent explicit instructions to follow the three-step call pattern before writing SQL: get_projects, then get_models, then get_semantics on the target model. Tell it to reference only attribute and metric names that get_semantics returned. Include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (Customer Lifetime Spend is the customer’s total across their history regardless of the current slice. Sports Share of Wallet is a ratio. And so on). This is the prompt engineering that pays the most in accuracy.

Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The get_semantics payload runs to a few thousand tokens and doesn’t change within a model version, so caching drops the input-token cost per call on repeated invocations. Agent traffic against a stable semantic layer is exactly the repetitive, bursty pattern that benefits most.

Two effects compound on the MCP path. First, get_semantics returns compressed business context (metric definitions, hierarchies, attribute forms) instead of raw schema DDL, so the model reasons over a smaller, higher-signal payload. Strategy’s published benchmark measures the input-token and per-query cost impact of serving semantic context versus raw schema. Second, Bedrock prompt caching keeps that already-compressed payload warm across calls. For repetitive agent traffic, both effects apply per call: the model reasons over compressed context, and repeat calls hit the cache.

Verification

To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three query categories through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them as a different role.

Query 1, Aurora-only. List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.

The agent generates a query against the Customer model that projects the display forms of Customer and City and filters state to WI:

SELECT "customer__customer name", "city__city name"
FROM   "Customer"
WHERE  "state__state name" = 'WI'
ORDER BY "customer__customer name"

Mosaic pushes a single query to Aurora and returns the rows. Amazon Redshift is not touched.

Query 2, Amazon Redshift only. What are our top 10 products by units sold?

SELECT "product__product name", SUM("Units Sold") AS "total_units"
FROM   "Purchase"
GROUP BY "product__product name"
ORDER BY "total_units" DESC
LIMIT 10

The entire query pushes to Amazon Redshift. Aurora is not touched.

Query 3, cross-model. Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?

SELECT "customer__customer name",
       "state__state name",
       SUM("Customer Lifetime Spend") AS "lifetime_spend"
FROM   "Customer"
WHERE  "rewards_account__account_id" IS NULL
GROUP BY "customer__customer name", "state__state name"
ORDER BY "lifetime_spend" DESC
LIMIT 20

Mosaic plans across both models. Profile and enrollment status come from Aurora, spend aggregation from Amazon Redshift, joined on the Customer linking attribute inside the Mosaic engine, then filtered and top-N’d. The agent did not need to define Customer Lifetime Spend. It referenced the metric by name and Mosaic resolved the formula, level qualifier, and linking paths.

Governance rerun. We ran Query 1 with ssn added to the projection as two callers. As a fraud analyst, get_semantics returned the SSN attribute and the query returned the values. As a marketing analyst, get_semantics returned a Customer attribute without ssn at all, so the agent had no attribute to project. Same request, same query text, two correct answers from one definition.

Cross-interface confirmation. We opened the same certified Customer model in Excel through the Mosaic XMLA endpoint and dragged State and Customer Lifetime Spend onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals matched the agent’s numbers exactly.

Early in the run, the agent averaged share of wallet across customers, the classic non-additive mistake. Adding one line to the metric description (“ratio metric. Do not average across customers, recompute from components”) stopped it. That’s the case for writing metric descriptions in the first sprint rather than the last.

Extending across data sources

The same linking mechanism extends to a third source: clickstream events in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) queried through Amazon Athena, tables in Apache Iceberg on Amazon S3 Tables, a capability of Amazon S3, or a SaaS source such as a CRM. Model the source in Mosaic, link it on Customer and Time, and browse-to-buy questions compose into the same customer view without a third pipeline. Adding a source doesn’t change the metric definitions that already exist. The agent can only travel paths a modeler declared. AWS Lake Formation governs access to the underlying lake tables. Mosaic’s RLS and OLS apply on top.

The same live-source pattern applies to every system in Strategy’s supported data source catalog, covering on-premises databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL alongside the warehouses and engines already named in this post.

Interoperability with Apache Ossie

Some tools will not take a dependency on a single semantic layer. Apache Ossie (incubating) is the open specification for that gap, launched as the Open Semantic Interchange on September 23, 2025 and now in the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie (incubating). It defines a vendor-neutral format for metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business concepts so definitions move between tools without being retyped. Strategy participates alongside Snowflake, Dremio, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and others.

Mosaic exports and imports Ossie artifacts. Metric and dimension definitions modeled over Amazon Redshift publish as Ossie YAML consumable by Ossie-aware tools without a Mosaic connector. Definitions authored elsewhere (a metric maintained in dbt, a dimension standardized in a catalog) flow into Mosaic instead of being re-implemented. The artifacts are plain text, so they live in Git and promote through environments like other code.

Apache Ossie is early. Use it where portability matters most and fidelity matters least, for example formulas, dimensions, descriptions, and ownership metadata, while keeping governance policy, execution strategy, and security configuration native to Mosaic.

Deployment: Strategy Cloud

Mosaic runs as a managed service on Strategy Cloud. Strategy operates the application. Connections to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora go over the network from Strategy Cloud egress. You allow-list the Strategy Cloud CIDRs on the source security groups.

Observability

Two observability planes cover the path from question to answer.

Sentinel and Platform Analytics cover the query side. Sentinel captures near real-time query duration, slow queries, and usage by user, tool, and model.

AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, covers the agent side: planning steps, tool calls, latency per turn. Sentinel and Platform Analytics show what happened once the request reached Mosaic. AgentCore Observability shows what the agent was doing before it got there.

Conclusion

Reliable agentic analytics combines strong reasoning, trusted business context, and secure execution. Amazon Bedrock provides the model, Strategy Mosaic provides the governed semantic layer over live data, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent and terminates authentication. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not to Amazon Redshift or Aurora directly. Schemas evolve, the semantic model absorbs the change, and the same definitions serve Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, the Strands agent, and Amazon Quick. Through Apache Ossie, they also reach tools that do not connect to Mosaic.

Where to start

  • Pick one metric currently argued about (NRR, contribution margin, active customer are common candidates). One metric with more than one definition in circulation.
  • Write three to five business questions about it. These become your acceptance tests.
  • Model your primary source in Mosaic and get the metric returning a defensible number.
  • Link additional sources incrementally, one at a time, on the attributes that already exist in the model.
  • Author descriptions on every metric and attribute the agent will see. This is where accuracy moves most.
  • Connect the Strands agent over Mosaic MCP and run your acceptance questions.
  • Observe real query patterns for a couple of weeks, then move what’s hot to in-memory.
  • Export stable definitions to Apache Ossie and put them under version control.

Further reading

  • Strategy Mosaic – Universal Semantic Layer
  • Interact with Agents, Mosaic Models, and Cubes Using an MCP Server
  • Strategy Advanced Metrics: Report Data and Calculations
  • Strategy Conditional Metrics
  • Strategy Metric Level Symbols
  • Strategy Compound Metrics
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
  • Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
  • Apache Ossie (incubating)
  • Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
  • Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

About the authors

Zhili Cheng

Zhili is a Principal Product Manager at Strategy, leading Mosaic, the universal semantic layer from Strategy, with 17+ years spanning engineering and product.

George Earle

George is the Director of AI Engineering at Strategy, where he leads the company’s AI engineering efforts.

Kyle K

Kyle is an experienced Sales Engineer in enterprise software, specializing in pre-sales, solution architecture, and proof-of-concept engagements. He holds a B.S. in Computer Science from Eastern Washington University.

JP Boreddy

JP is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, where he partners with enterprise customers on cloud architecture, data, and AI workloads.

Sahil Thapar

Sahil is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, where he works with ISV customers to build highly available, scalable, and resilient applications on the AWS Cloud. He specializes in containers, machine learning, and generative AI, helping enterprises architect production-grade solutions.

item.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Frank Lapolito
item.description: The third post in our semantic-layer series builds a governed customer 360 model on Amazon Redshift with AtScale, then exposes it to a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore through the AtScale MCP server. Identity propagation, RBAC, row security, and full query audit are enforced at the semantic layer, not the prompt.
item.content:encoded:
In the first post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. We ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with AtScale as the semantic layer.

AtScale takes a different shape from the first two. The semantic model is dimensional (dimensions, hierarchies, and measures) rather than a graph of triples or a set of views. AtScale authors the model in the Semantic Modeling Language, an open, YAML-based specification versioned in Git, and exposes it simultaneously, from a single deployed model, over three protocols: SQL, XML for Analysis (XMLA), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The Strands agent and the business intelligence (BI) tools the enterprise already uses get the same computed answer from the same definitions.

The rest of the pattern carries over from the earlier posts. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the walkthrough) plans and writes queries. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the Strands agent and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to AtScale. The joins, metric definitions, and row and column filters that apply to the caller live inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt.

We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series: what a semantic layer is, what it’s for, and why the model plans queries without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the first post covers the ground.

By the end of this post, you will know:

  • How to model a C360 domain in the Semantic Modeling Language (SML): datasets, dimensions and hierarchies, facts, measures, calculated measures, and perspectives, versioned in Git.
  • How AtScale plans a dimensional query against Amazon Redshift, and how AtScale’s autonomous aggregate management accelerates the query patterns an agent generates.
  • How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the AtScale MCP server, and how to register that MCP server with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • How the human user’s identity propagates from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to AtScale, and how AtScale enforces role-based access control (RBAC), row security, and perspectives at query time.
  • How to deploy AtScale on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository.

The source of truth for the walkthrough is the AtScale C2026.7 release. Where a specific tool name or endpoint applies, we cite the AtScale documentation.

The example: Customer 360 on Amazon Redshift

The customer 360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. A retail enterprise has customer records, orders, products, and rewards enrollments spread across systems, and business users want to ask cross-cutting questions without knowing which system holds which fact. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit we adapted for the first post in the series models this scenario with Customer, Order, Product, and Address entities joined on an integer cid that appears as a primary key in the customer table and as a plain column in the purchase table.

Where this post differs from the first two is where the data physically sits. Stardog and Denodo federate at query time across two engines. AtScale plans a dimensional query as native warehouse SQL and pushes it to one engine per query, so cross-engine data is consolidated upstream. For this walkthrough, all analytical C360 data lives in Amazon Redshift Serverless. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL remains the operational system of record, and a replication path (AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL to Amazon Redshift) keeps the analytical copy current. The agent queries a single AtScale model that maps to the Amazon Redshift tables.

The schema in Amazon Redshift:

Table Key columns
customer cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location
address id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name
credit_card id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type
rewards_account id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date
purchase id (PK), pid, purchase_date, quantity, price, cid, card
product id (PK), name, brand, price, dept
category id (PK), dept_name, parent
vendor id (PK), vendor_name, industry

Nine columns of interest across eight tables. cid links customer records to purchases. pid links purchases to products. dept links products to categories. Everything analytical is in Amazon Redshift, so joins push down to native SQL rather than being resolved in the semantic layer or in an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline.

A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post, carried over so a reader following the series can see the same request answered by a different semantic layer. It touches customer profile, address, purchase history, and enrollment status: one row per customer across four logical entities.

AtScale terms used in this post

AtScale implements the semantic layer as a dimensional model over a warehouse. The AtScale documentation and the SML specification use a specific set of primitives that come up throughout this post. A short reference is useful before we get to the walkthrough.

  • Semantic Modeling Language (SML) – An open, YAML-based specification for describing semantic models. Every SML object (model, dataset, dimension, hierarchy, metric, calculation, perspective, row security) is a YAML file. The specification lives at github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML.
  • Model – The top-level artifact. A model references datasets, dimensions, facts, and metrics, and exposes them through the AtScale query engine.
  • Dimension and hierarchy – A dimension groups related attributes (customer, product, date). A hierarchy inside a dimension organizes those attributes into levels (product → category → department, or year → quarter → month → day).
  • Fact and measure – A fact is a dataset that holds measurable events joined to dimensions on key columns. A measure is a quantity aggregated from a fact column, for example SUM(price * quantity) for revenue.
  • Calculation – A derived measure expressed as a formula against other measures.
  • Perspective – A publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group. Perspectives are how AtScale controls which dimensions and measures a caller can see.
  • Row security – A model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes.
  • Autonomous aggregate management – AtScale watches query patterns across consumers and materializes summary tables in the warehouse when a pattern is expensive enough to justify one. Subsequent queries that match the pattern route to the aggregate transparently.
  • Design Center – The AtScale authoring surface. A modeler edits SML through a visual canvas or a text editor. Either way the artifact on disk is SML YAML in Git.
  • AtScale MCP server – The in-product MCP endpoint at <atscale-host>/mcp that exposes the semantic model to any MCP client.

Where more detail is useful, the AtScale documentation and the SML specification are the authoritative references.

Reference architecture

The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path, following the same shape as the Stardog and Denodo posts.

Inbound. A client sends the user’s question to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to AgentCore runtime (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), which hosts the agent process. The agent invokes Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.

Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, it invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server. AgentCore Gateway serves as the outbound proxy: the AtScale MCP server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls route through Gateway and AgentCore Identity injects the credential at that hop. AtScale’s MCP endpoint accepts either a bearer token (for development and single-identity scenarios) or an OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak instance (the production path). The AtScale engine validates the token, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query against the deployed C360 model.

The query request travels down through the AtScale engine, and the results travel back up. There’s no ETL job that pre-materializes cross-database joins. The analytical copy in Amazon Redshift is the source of truth for the semantic model, kept fresh from Aurora by the upstream replication path.

Figure 1: Inbound authentication path and outbound query path between the client, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components, the AtScale MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift Serverless

The architecture is deliberately opinionated on identity. Gateway and Identity hold the tokens at the runtime edges. The agent doesn’t see them and only orchestrates the conversation and the tool calls.

Build the semantic layer

AtScale’s semantic model is a collection of SML objects (datasets, dimensions, facts, measures, calculations, perspectives, row security) versioned in Git. A working model has a shape a data engineer will recognize from a star schema, but every object is expressed as YAML rather than data definition language (DDL), and every object is a separate file. Building the C360 model happens in three passes: datasets over the Amazon Redshift tables, dimensions and hierarchies with the joins between them, and measures and calculations that express the business logic.

Datasets. Each Amazon Redshift table becomes an SML dataset. A dataset declares the physical connection, the schema, the table, and the columns AtScale will surface. Datasets can be authored visually in Design Center or edited directly as YAML. Either surface writes the same SML file to Git.

Dimensions and hierarchies. The C360 model has seven dimensions. dim_customer holds customer profile attributes and joins to dim_address through the location key and to dim_rewards through cid. dim_product holds product attributes and organizes them into a hierarchy through dim_category. dim_date supports date-based analysis. dim_vendor groups products by supplier. dim_rewards holds one row per enrolled customer with account_id and create_date, and snowflakes off dim_customer so that never-enrolled customers surface as null in the enrollment attributes.

AtScale’s hierarchy primitive is the concise expression of the product-to-category relationship. A query against the model can navigate product → category → parent category without a recursive SQL common table expression, and the large language model (LLM) sees a single dimensional path rather than a join graph.

A representative SML fragment for the product hierarchy:

# dim_product.yml
unique_name: dim_product
object_type: dimension
label: Product
hierarchies:
  - unique_name: product_category
    label: Product Category
    levels:
      - unique_name: department
        dataset: category
        key_columns: [dept_name]
      - unique_name: category
        dataset: category
        key_columns: [id]
      - unique_name: product
        dataset: product
        key_columns: [id]
secondary_attributes:
  - unique_name: brand
  - unique_name: product_name
    key_column: name

Facts and measures. The fact table for C360 is fact_purchase, mapped to the Amazon Redshift purchase table. It joins to dim_customer on cid, to dim_product on pid, and to dim_date on purchase_date. Measures come off the fact: total_revenue as SUM(price * quantity), order_count as COUNT(id), and units_sold as SUM(quantity).

Calculated measures. Business logic that lives in the model rather than in the query. customer_lifetime_value is total_revenue evaluated at customer grain, the same formula applied to a coarser slice of the fact. Segments like big_spender and spend_tier are calculated measures with conditional expressions:

# big_spender.yml
unique_name: big_spender
object_type: metric
expression: |
  CASE WHEN SUM(price * quantity) > 10000
  THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END

The expression is evaluated at query time. A column would hold one answer at one grain. The expression recomputes for whatever slice the query asks about, by customer, by customer and year, or by region. When the definition changes (the threshold moves from $10,000 to $15,000), the update happens in one YAML file, gets reviewed as a pull request, and deploys through the AtScale CI hook. Each consumer picks up the new definition on the next query, whether that is the agent, Excel over XMLA, or Tableau over Multidimensional Expressions (MDX).

Figure 2: The C360 model in AtScale Design Center. dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, dim_product with the product-to-category hierarchy, dim_date, dim_vendor, and fact_purchase connected by orange lines that indicate dimension-to-fact and snowflake relationships. Calculated measures (customer_lifetime_value, big_spender, spend_tier) appear as separate nodes referenced from the fact

Figure 3: The same model as side-by-side SML YAML, one file per dimension, metric, and calculation, versioned in a Git repository

The artifact on the right of Figure 3 is not a description of the model. It is the model. Design Center’s visual canvas and the YAML editor are two views of the same file, and the Git diff is the authoritative record of every change. The files conform to the open-source SML specification, so the repository can be read without the engine.

After it’s deployed, the model is simultaneously reachable over SQL (for JDBC-based BI tools and notebooks), XMLA (for Excel and Power BI), and MCP (for the agent). The total_revenue calculation returns the same number to Claude Sonnet 4.6 as it does to an Excel PivotTable pointed at the same XMLA endpoint. We confirm this match in Verification.

How AtScale plans and pushes down queries

When the agent asks a question against the semantic model, AtScale’s AI Computation Engine (ACE) does the planning. The steps a query goes through are the same for a dimensional SQL request from the MCP run_query tool and for an XMLA request from Excel. Only the parser at the front differs.

Take the auto-enrollment question: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? The agent, prompted with the model context returned by describe_model, composes a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model. ACE parses that query into a logical plan, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying fact_purchase, dim_customer, dim_address, and dim_rewards datasets, applies any row security the caller is subject to, and then plans the physical query against Amazon Redshift.

Two things happen at the physical-planning stage that separate AtScale from a hand-written pipeline. First, the join is pushed to Amazon Redshift as a native SQL join rather than materialized in the semantic layer. The Amazon Redshift optimizer sees a single SQL statement with a filter and an aggregate, and executes it accordingly. Second, AtScale’s aggregate manager checks its registry for a pre-built aggregate that matches the query pattern. If a summary table exists that groups purchases by customer at the right grain, AtScale rewrites the query to hit the aggregate instead of scanning fact_purchase. The query returns in a fraction of the time it would take against the raw fact table, without the agent or the modeler doing any manual work to route it.

Figure 4: The agent’s dimensional query enters the AtScale planner. The planner checks its aggregate registry, finds a matching aggregate for the query pattern, rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift, and returns the result. The lower path shows the same query without a matching aggregate hitting fact_purchase directly

The aggregate manager is what makes an agent-driven workload economically feasible. LLM-driven analysis fires more queries than a human analyst would, and open-ended prompts like Tell me something interesting about our sales can spawn a dozen. AtScale watches the query pattern, materializes aggregates in the warehouse itself (not a separate cache), and routes matching queries transparently. Aggregate creation is demand-defined against observed traffic across consumers, not only the agent.

The audit record for the query captures both the dimensional SQL the LLM wrote and the warehouse-native SQL AtScale rewrote it into, along with whether an aggregate served the query. That record is available to an operator through the AtScale Queries page in Design Center, and it’s what the following governance section builds on.

A note on multi-source and interoperability

AtScale connects to warehouses over JDBC. The C360 walkthrough targets Amazon Redshift Serverless. The same SML model works over Snowflake, Databricks, and Google BigQuery, and AtScale documents the connection pattern for each. What changes when you swap the connection is the SQL dialect AtScale emits, not the SML in Git.

One architectural property is worth stating explicitly because it differs from the first two posts in this series. A single AtScale query resolves in one warehouse engine. If the C360 model spans two warehouses (dimensions on Snowflake, facts on Amazon Redshift, say), a query that touches both must be reconciled in one of two ways. The first is upstream, by consolidating an analytical copy in one warehouse through a replication path. The second is by the warehouse itself, using engine-level federation such as Amazon Redshift Spectrum for querying Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or Apache Iceberg tables that both engines can read. AtScale plans a dimensional query and pushes it to one engine. The cross-engine story lives one layer down.

That choice cuts both ways. It rules out the live cross-engine federation Stardog and Denodo perform at query time, but it lets AtScale’s planner and aggregate manager work against a single-engine execution model, which is what makes the aggregate story load-bearing at scale. Enterprises that already run a warehouse-centric analytical architecture with change data capture (CDC) pipelines from operational systems reuse that architecture. Enterprises whose answers require live federation across engines are better served by the semantic layers in the first two posts.

Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement

Customer 360 data is regulated. Some users (HR, fraud) need to see personally identifiable information such as Social Security numbers and card numbers. Most users (marketing, analytics) must not. Row-level filters restrict analysts by geography, and a per-user audit trail must survive from the human’s browser through to the warehouse.

AtScale enforces these requirements at the semantic layer, before any query reaches the warehouse. Enforcement happens identically whether the caller is the Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One row-security object in SML, one perspective, one set of role bindings, applied to each consumer of the model.

Identity propagation from the user to AtScale

The chain follows the same shape as the one in the Denodo post, with the terminal hop landing at the AtScale engine rather than continuing to the warehouse.

  1. The human authenticates to the application against the enterprise IdP and receives a JWT.
  2. The application forwards the JWT as a bearer token to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway, which validates it (issuer, audience, signature) and routes the request to AgentCore runtime.
  3. When the agent invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server, AgentCore Identity supplies the OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak, mapped to the human user’s identity. The AtScale credential does not enter agent code.
  4. The AtScale MCP server accepts the OAuth token. The AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query with the caller’s row-security constraints and perspective bindings applied. The warehouse is reached with the AtScale connection identity from AWS Secrets Manager.

Figure 5: The identity chain from human user through AgentCore Gateway, AgentCore runtime, AgentCore Identity, the AtScale MCP server, and the AtScale engine, terminating at the semantic-layer enforcement point. The warehouse hop is a service-account connection with the AtScale credential

RBAC, row security, and perspectives

AtScale expresses access control as three composable primitives. RBAC assigns roles to callers based on Keycloak claims. Row security is a model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. A perspective is a publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group.

For the C360 walkthrough, we define two roles.

  • hr_user: sees the full C360 model, including ssn and card_num.
  • marketing_user: sees the Marketing perspective, which hides ssn and card_num at the model layer.

When marketing_user asks a question that references ssn, the agent’s describe_model call returns the Marketing perspective, one that does not include ssn. The agent has no attribute to project. Row-level filters compose the same way: an SML row-security object that scopes customers by state restricts a caller to a specific set of rows without any change to the agent’s prompt.

Audit fidelity

Queries through the AtScale engine are logged with the caller’s identity, the model, the LLM-generated dimensional SQL, the AtScale-translated pushdown SQL that Amazon Redshift saw, the security policies applied, whether an aggregate served the query, and the row count returned. Because the record captures both the query the model wrote and the query the warehouse executed, an auditor can trace an answer from the human question to the SQL that produced the number. Neither the first nor the second post in this series captures both forms of the query in one record.

An audit record for a governed query looks like this:

{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-31T10:34:56Z",
  "user_identity": "mary_major@example.com",
  "user_role": "marketing_user",
  "semantic_model": "Customer_360",
  "question": "Top 10 customers by revenue in California",
  "generated_sql": "SELECT full_name, total_revenue FROM ...",
  "translated_pushdown_sql": "SELECT ... FROM redshift ...",
  "security_policies_applied": ["regional_row_security"],
  "served_from": "aggregate",
  "execution_time_ms": 850,
  "rows_returned": 10
}

The generated_sql and translated_pushdown_sql fields are the ones that make the trail complete: an auditor sees both the query the LLM composed against the semantic model and the query the warehouse actually ran.

Expose the layer through the AtScale MCP server

The AtScale MCP server is a component of the AtScale distribution, exposed at <atscale-host>/mcp. It’s generally available in the AtScale C2026.7 release and speaks the standard Model Context Protocol. Any MCP-compatible client (the Strands agent in AgentCore runtime, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code) can connect to the same endpoint against the same deployed model.

The server exposes a set of tools scoped to querying the semantic model. The AtScale documentation publishes a tools reference per release. The tools that matter for an agent-driven workload are:

  • list_models: Enumerate the models the caller can see, along with the column groups that describe how dimensions map to facts.
  • describe_model: Return the dimensions, hierarchies, measures, calculations, and business descriptions for a chosen model. This is the payload the agent’s system prompt is loaded with before it starts composing queries.
  • search_columns: Keyword search over the model’s columns. Useful when a full describe_model payload would use too much of the LLM’s context window.
  • validate_query: Check that a dimensional SQL statement is compatible with the model without executing it against the warehouse. This lets the agent iterate on its query cheaply before firing anything Amazon Redshift will bill for.
  • run_query: Execute a dimensional SQL statement against the model and return the rows.
  • run_queries: Run multiple statements in a batch, useful for open-ended prompts where the agent fires several exploratory queries in parallel.
  • get_version: Report the MCP server version, so a client can decide whether to cache the model schema.

The AtScale MCP endpoint accepts two authentication modes. The bearer-token path uses an API token minted from Design Center. Every request runs as the token owner, and this path suits a proof-of-concept or a single-identity service. The OAuth 2.0 path uses AtScale’s bundled Keycloak with a pre-provisioned client whose ID is exactly atscale-mcp, documented on the AtScale Connecting with Claude page. AgentCore Gateway presents the access token on the agent’s behalf, the AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, and downstream policy evaluation uses the human user’s identity.

Registering the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target follows the standard Gateway MCP target flow. The tools listed earlier appear to the agent as ordinary tools, with AgentCore Identity handling the credential at the Gateway hop.

Sidebar: Extending the model with AI-assisted modeling

The AtScale MCP server exposes tools scoped to querying, and AtScale has been extending the MCP surface with author-side tools that let an agent introspect a warehouse schema, generate a candidate SML model from source metadata, validate the SML against the specification, and commit the result to Git. This pattern, in which an agent shapes the semantic model rather than only reading from it, is a natural fit for Claude Code and Cursor workflows. In those workflows, a data engineer collaborates with the LLM to bootstrap a model over a new dataset.

AtScale groups this direction into three capabilities. A Semantic Discovery Engine scans warehouse schemas, query history, and lineage to infer candidate joins, hierarchies, and metric definitions. A Model Recommendation System suggests dimensions, measures, and relationships based on observed query patterns. A Governed Feedback Loop keeps human review of AI suggestions in the SML-and-Git workflow, so changes are versioned and auditable.

The specific tools available at the time of publication are documented in the AtScale MCP tools reference. Check the current release notes for what is generally available and what is still in preview. The rest of this post covers the consumer path, an agent querying a deployed model, which is what a production C360 workflow relies on today.

Deploy and run the agent

Strands Agents is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the AtScale MCP server as a tool source. AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and holds the outbound AtScale credential through AgentCore Identity. Foundation model availability on Amazon Bedrock varies by AWS Region. For the current list, see Regional availability by models.

The system prompt matters. The AtScale documentation and the reference demos in the AtScale corpus consistently recommend a three-step call pattern for the agent: list_models to see what is available, then describe_model on the target model to load the dimensions and measures into context, and only then run_query (or validate_query first, if the query is expensive to iterate on). The reasoning is that the LLM should not fabricate column names or metric names. It should reference only what describe_model returned. The system prompt should say so explicitly, and it should include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (total_revenue means sales dollars, not units) so the agent maps user questions to the right measure.

Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The describe_model payload runs to a few thousand tokens and does not change within a model version, so caching it drops the input-token cost per query on repeated calls. The cache-point configuration is a request parameter on the BedrockModel object. See the Strands documentation for the current parameter name.

Verification

To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three queries through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them under a different role. The following behavior is what should reproduce in a working deployment.

Query 1, single dimension

List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.

The agent generates a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model that selects first_name, last_name, and city from dim_customer and dim_address where state = 'WI'. AtScale’s planner resolves the dimensional path to the customer and address tables in Amazon Redshift, pushes a single SQL statement down, and returns the rows.

Query 2, aggregation with aggregate hit

What are our top 10 products by units sold?

The agent aggregates units_sold by product and orders descending. AtScale’s aggregate manager finds a matching demand-defined aggregate and rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift rather than scanning fact_purchase. The Queries page shows both the LLM-generated dimensional SQL and the aggregate-routed warehouse SQL side by side.

Query 3, cross-domain

Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?

The agent generates a query that joins dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, and fact_purchase, and aggregates customer_lifetime_value by customer. The query restricts to customers where dim_rewards.account_id is null. The left join to dim_customer on cid keeps never-enrolled customers, who surface with a null enrollment record. The agent returns the top 20 by lifetime spend. AtScale’s planner resolves the joins to native SQL against Amazon Redshift and returns the ranked list. The customer_lifetime_value formula is not something the LLM had to invent. It’s a calculated measure defined once in customer_lifetime_value.yml and referenced by name in the query.

Governance rerun

We run a variant of Query 1 that adds ssn to the projection (Show me our customers in Wisconsin, with their SSN) as two different callers. As hr_user, describe_model returns the full C360 model, the agent composes the query, and the result set includes the SSN values. As marketing_user, describe_model returns the Marketing perspective, which does not expose ssn. The agent has no attribute to project, so it returns an answer without SSN. Nothing changes between the two runs except the caller’s identity. The query text, the agent code, the MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift are all untouched.

Cross-consumer confirmation

We opened the same C360 model in Excel through the AtScale XMLA endpoint and dragged Customer.State and Total Revenue onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals match the ones the agent returned for equivalent questions, to the exact number.

Extending across data sources

Adding a new data source to the C360 model is a modeling exercise, not an integration one. Suppose the customer support team asks that the model include ticket volumes so an agent can answer Which of our top spenders opened a support ticket in the last 30 days? The steps are:

  1. Land the support-ticket data in Amazon Redshift alongside the other C360 tables, using the same replication pattern used for the operational tables.
  2. Add an SML dataset that maps the new table to a logical object.
  3. Add or extend a dimension (dim_ticket) and add the join to dim_customer on cid.
  4. Add any new measures the model needs (open_ticket_count, avg_resolution_time).
  5. Commit the SML changes, review them as a pull request, and deploy through the AtScale CI hook.

Nothing changes in the agent code or the AgentCore configuration. The next time the agent calls describe_model, it sees the new dimension and measures, and it can compose questions against them. The same pattern applies to a different warehouse. If a source lands in Snowflake or Databricks rather than Amazon Redshift, the connection is a new SML dataset with a Snowflake or Databricks connection, and queries resolve in that engine per the earlier multi-source note.

Deployment: AtScale on Amazon EKS

AtScale runs on Kubernetes, and the reference deployment on AWS is Amazon EKS. AtScale ships an official Helm chart at oci://docker.io/atscaleinc/atscale, and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository provides infrastructure as code (IaC) scaffolding for standing up an EKS cluster with the components AtScale expects: an ingress controller, a persistent store for the AtScale metadata database, a Redis instance for query caching, and an AtScale-configured Keycloak instance for identity federation.

The AtScale deployment on EKS runs across a small set of Kubernetes pods. atscale-engine is the core query planner and executor. atscale-mcp-server is the MCP endpoint the agent talks to. atscale-keycloak is the bundled identity provider that federates to Amazon Cognito, Okta, Azure Active Directory, and other OpenID Connect (OIDC)-compliant IdPs. Supporting pods handle the SML API and the Design Center UI (atscale-sml-api, atscale-sml-web), PostgreSQL metadata storage (atscale-db), the query cache (atscale-redis), and ingress (atscale-ingress, typically fronted by an AWS Network Load Balancer).

The C360 application (a chat UI or a client library that calls the agent) can run in the same EKS cluster in its own namespace. It uses an IAM role for service account (IRSA) to reach Bedrock and AWS Secrets Manager without embedding credentials.

Networking is standard: AtScale reaches Amazon Redshift through the virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint or a security-group rule that permits the AtScale namespace’s egress to Amazon Redshift, and the human user reaches the application through the ingress load balancer.

AtScale offers cloud deployment options beyond self-managed EKS. Check the AtScale website for current offerings and AWS availability. The rest of this post assumes the self-managed pattern described earlier.

Conclusion

Agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that computes governed, business-meaningful answers over the live warehouse, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, AtScale, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.

The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the warehouse. Dimensions, hierarchies, measures, perspectives, and row security live in SML in Git. When a schema drifts or a governance rule changes, the update happens in one file, and each consumer (the agent, Excel, Tableau, Power BI) picks it up on the next query.

Where to start

Most teams that get this working start narrow and expand.

  1. Pick one workflow that spans two or three data sources and takes longer than it should to answer today.
  2. Write 3–5 questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer has to support on day one.
  3. Consolidate the analytical data into Amazon Redshift (or the warehouse of your choice), using AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL for operational data.
  4. Bootstrap the SML from the warehouse schema in Design Center, then refine it against the competency questions.
  5. Deploy AtScale on Amazon EKS with the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints, register the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target, and wire a Strands agent through it.

Further reading

  • AtScale MCP server documentation: Connect to AtScale with AI
  • AtScale C2026.7 release notes: documentation.atscale.com
  • AtScale MCP tools reference (published per release with the AtScale documentation)
  • AtScale K8S Blueprints: github.com/AtScaleInc/atscale-k8s-blueprints
  • Semantic Modeling Language specification: github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
  • Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
  • Strands Agents on AWS Prescriptive Guidance
  • Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (first post in this series)
  • Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (second post in this series)
